Kill switch, step 2 of the desktop plan - the Windows block: WindowsVpnKillSwitch, the Windows Filtering Platform's own filters under a provider and a sublayer of ours, persistent, so the block holds through a crash of the service and a reboot, loaded at boot before any app starts; every change is one transaction with no gap. The connect and accept layers (ALE, once per connection) let through, highest weight first, the service (its exe as SYSTEM, not the window's run of it), the tunnel's interface (the WinTun adapter's LUID, by its GUID, re-pointed at each adapter start), loopback, DHCP and NDP, an out-of-tunnel plan's resolvers, then block DNS - a LAN router's too - then the device-level split, then block the rest; the forward layers let forwarded traffic into and out of the tunnel and to the split only. The provider's data names the app whose block it is by its exe, so a person's disconnect lifts only its own; the filters' keys are a fixed base with an index, so a removal finds every one. The interop's layouts and GUIDs follow the Windows SDK's fwpmtypes.h and fwpmu.h. With the switch on, the service asks the network's resolvers for the server's name itself (EndPointResolver, DnsUtils.GetNetworkDnsServers), as Windows' resolver asks from a process the block stops. `vhclient kill-switch on|off`, beside always-on, through the service Tested: on the Windows 10 and Windows Server 2025 Desktop VMs against the server VM - connected, the tunnel and the LAN split pass and DNS to the LAN router is blocked; the service killed, after its restart and after an error stop, the internet and DNS are blocked (WSAEACCES) and the LAN split passes; a reboot while blocked keeps it from boot; a person's disconnect lifts it at once; the switch off and on during a session lifts it and puts it back with the session kept. A new EndPointResolverTests case for the in-process lookup, the whole VpnHood.Test and VpnHood.AppLib.Test (but VpnTunnelLockTest's three OS-lock tests, which another app's tunnel lock fails here, elevated too).
